name: Huastecan
region: The Huasteca on the Gulf coast of Mexico (Veracruz and San Luis Potosí); Chicomuseltec in Chiapas
defining_innovation: The first branch to leave, and the only Mayan language far from the Maya area: Huastec (Teenek) is spoken hundreds of kilometres north of any other Mayan language.

chapters.title: Far to the North
chapters.body:
Huastec, whose speakers call it *Teenek*, is spoken in the Huasteca region of the Mexican Gulf coast, separated from all other Mayan languages by Nahuatl- and Totonac-speaking areas. It split from the rest of Mayan earliest, and how its speakers came to be so far north is not known: they may have moved up the coast, or the Mayan languages in between may have been replaced.

Its closest relative, Chicomuseltec, was spoken in Chiapas near the Guatemalan border and became extinct in the late 20th century. Huastec itself is still spoken by around 170,000 people, and in the 15th century the Huastec region was conquered by the Aztecs and absorbed many Nahuatl loanwords.

chapters.title: Teenek Today
chapters.body:
Huastec, or Teenek, is spoken in two main areas: the eastern part of the state of San Luis Potosí, around towns such as Tancanhuitz and Aquismón, and northern Veracruz, around Tantoyuca. The two varieties differ enough in sounds and vocabulary to be treated as separate dialects, and some classifications count them as separate languages. Mexico's 2020 census recorded about 170,000 speakers aged three and over.

Over three thousand years of separation have made Huastec the most divergent Mayan language. It has lost the uvular stops of Proto-Mayan, merging them with *k*, and it has developed rounded velar consonants, *kw* and *k'w*, found nowhere else in the family. Its vocabulary also carries the marks of long contact with Nahuatl, whose speakers share the Huasteca region.

Since 2003 Huastec has been one of Mexico's recognised national languages under the General Law of Linguistic Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and it is taught in bilingual primary schools. As elsewhere, children increasingly grow up speaking Spanish, and language shift is more advanced in some communities than in others.

speakers.note: All speakers of Huastec; Chicomuseltec is extinct.

sources.citation: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (INEGI). 2021. Censo de Población y Vivienda 2020. Aguascalientes: INEGI.
Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.

turning_points.title: To the Gulf coast
turning_points.description: The ancestors of the Huastec separate from the other Mayan speakers and end up on the northern Gulf coast. The route and the date are unknown, and glottochronological estimates are unreliable.

sources.citation: Kaufman, Terrence. 1976. Archaeological and linguistic correlations in Mayaland and associated areas of Meso-America. World Archaeology 8(1).

turning_points.title: Aztec conquest and Nahuatl
turning_points.description: The Aztec empire conquers the Huasteca, and Nahuatl becomes a neighbouring and administrative language. Huastec absorbs Nahuatl vocabulary, and Nahuatl-speaking communities settle within the region.

sources.citation: Aissen, Judith, Nora C. England & Roberto Zavala Maldonado, eds. 2017. The Mayan Languages. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Chicomuseltec falls silent
turning_points.description: Chicomuseltec, the only other Huastecan language, loses its last speakers in Chiapas. It is documented only in short word lists and notes.

sources.citation: Campbell, Lyle & Terrence Kaufman. 1985. Mayan linguistics: Where are we now? Annual Review of Anthropology 14.
